newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM urges belt tightening to help economy.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM urges belt tightening to help economy.

text.p: Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh on Tuesday urged Thai people to tighten their belts, stop spending money unecessarily and save more in order to help improve the sagging economy.
"We spend a lot. We buy everything. All Thai people spend a lot of money," Chavalit told the Foreign Correspondents Club. "Now we are in trouble. All people must tighten their belts."
Chavalit said top priorities for his six-week old government were to speed up the slowing economy and narrow the ballooning current account deficit.
Thailand's economic growth slowed to about 6.7 percent last year -- a sharp drop from the past decade when its growth was among the highest in the world averaging over nine percent a year.
Slow exports, rising imports and lower savings caused the current account deficit to reach an estimated 8.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996 -- among the highest in the region.
To help solve the problems, Chavalit urged Thais to save more, saying household savings had now dropped to between six and seven percent of GDP from 12 to 14 percent a few years ago.

Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan promised the government would cut all unnecessary spending -- especially on projects that are not seen to be immediately necessary to the economy's recovery and the country's growth.
The Chavalit administration has vowed to slash 50 billion baht ($2.0 billion) from the budget in each of the 1996/97 and 1997/97 (October to September) fiscal years.

"We aim to cut unnecessary spending. I might step on people's toes but public interest comes first," Amnuay said. "The idea is not cutting for cutting's sake. We want value out of our spending. If we see a lot of spending of public money that is wasteful we will cut it."
Amnuay said a total of about 80 billion baht of projects had been targetted for cancellation.
Commerce Minister Narongchai Akrasanee said he expected to see a sharp narrowing in the current account deficit as a percentage of GDP in 1997 over last year.

"The picture in 1997 will be different," he said. "You may be surprised that the current account deficit as a percentage of GDP in 1997 will be lower than what the Bank of Thailand predicted a few weeks ago."
The central bank has projected a current account deficit of 7.9 percent of GDP for 1997.
Chavalit said the overall goal for his government was to restore faith in the economy and speed up political reform.

"I want to lay the foundation for a healthy, vibrant society and economy," he said. "I want to leave office secure in the knowlege that subsequent governments will not have to come back to the same problems over and over again."
"Thailand has paid a high price for economic development," he said. "We must now refocus on the original purpose of development, which is to improve the quality of life."
